Temporal persistence diagrams — report on Result 2¶

Task 2 of the first stage. The subpackage tdadyn.zigzag: zigzag persistence on dynamic graphs and localisation of topological events in time.

This continues the Task 5 report (notebooks/report.ipynb). There the datasets were built whose correct answer is known in advance; here the algorithm is checked against them. The reader is assumed to know the first report: Betti numbers, persistent homology and the structure of family 2 are not retold below.

0. What was required and what came out¶

The criterion from the proposal: correct detection of events known in advance — births, merges, disappearance of cycles — on synthetic graphs with controlled dynamics; the metrics are event recall and precision and the localisation error in time.

In short, the outcome:
On the two family-2 datasets recall and precision 1.0, localisation error 0
The barcode computed twice, independently the oracle and Dionysus agreed on 3192 bars, 0 discrepancies
On the null model a false positive on 98.3% of snapshots — measured, not claimed
Under noise recall falls slowly, precision collapses to 0.17%

And — no less important — the report names what these metrics do not check. Section 8.

Then in order: what a topological event is (1), why ordinary persistence does not work here (2), how the zigzag is built (3–4), how the answer is obtained in two ways (5–6), how the barcode turns into events (7–8), and what happens when there is no truth or it is noisy (9–11).

Where the numbers come from¶

Not a single number below is computed in this notebook. All of them are read from the artefact produced by one command:

make results          # python -m tdadyn.results --config config.yaml --results

The artefact lives in data/synthetic/results/zigzag_events.json and is kept in git — it is not data but a record of a measurement: the datasets can be regenerated from the config and seed, while the statement "the report was written against these numbers" cannot. A rebuild gives the same content_sha256; only the timestamp changes.

The notebook loads the datasets only for illustrations: a drawn snapshot of a graph is not a reported quantity.

The HTML version loads MathJax from a CDN — without a network, formulas show as source text. Numbers, tables and figures do not depend on the network.

NOISY = [e for e in ART["datasets"] if e["kind"] == "noisy"]

def label(position):

1. A topological event: what exactly has to be found¶

A dynamic graph is a sequence of snapshots $G_0, \dots, G_{T-1}$ on one and the same vertex set. Between neighbouring snapshots edges appear and disappear, and with them topological features appear and disappear: connected components ($H_0$) and independent cycles ($H_1$).

An event is the moment a feature is born or dies. In the language of homology there are exactly two operations, birth and death: merging and splitting of classes do not exist in a barcode, and the intuitive "a cycle split in two" means, in this language, the birth of a new class.

The main dataset is cycle_lifecycle on 24 vertices and 60 snapshots. Its scenario is chosen so that every event follows from one understandable change of the graph.

In [2]:
from tdadyn.core import adjacency_from_snapshot, load_dataset

LIFECYCLE = load_dataset(next((ROOT / "dynamic_graph").glob("cycle_lifecycle_*")))
LOOP = load_dataset(next((ROOT / "dynamic_graph").glob("geometric_loop_*")))

def graph_at(dataset, snapshot):
    truth = dataset.ground_truth
    return adjacency_from_snapshot(dataset.snapshots[snapshot],
                                   edge_rule=truth.edge_rule,
                                   edge_threshold=truth.edge_threshold)

def draw_graph(ax, adjacency, title, highlight=(), n=None):
    n = n or adjacency.shape[0]
    angle = np.arange(n) * 2 * np.pi / n
    xy = np.c_[np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)]
    for i, j in zip(*np.triu_indices(n, 1)):
        if adjacency[i, j]:
            colour = "tab:red" if (i, j) in highlight else "tab:blue"
            width = 2.2 if (i, j) in highlight else 0.9
            ax.plot(*xy[[i, j]].T, color=colour, lw=width, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter(*xy.T, s=14, color="0.25", zorder=3)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")

STAGES = [(0, "snapshot 0: a path\n$\\beta_1 = 0$", ()),
          (12, "12: the path closed\nbirth of $H_1$", ((0, 23),)),
          (27, "27: a chord added\nbirth of a second $H_1$", ((0, 12),)),
          (41, "41: edge (6,7) removed\ndeath of $H_1$", ()),
          (48, "48: (3,4) removed\nbirth of $H_0$", ())]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(13.5, 3.0))
for ax, (snap, title, hi) in zip(axes, STAGES):
    draw_graph(ax, graph_at(LIFECYCLE, snap), title, highlight=hi)
fig.suptitle("cycle_lifecycle: five events over 60 snapshots", y=1.06, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Edges whose addition causes an event are shown in red. Note snapshot 27: the chord $(0,12)$ splits the 24-cycle into two cycles of length 13; in the language of graphs this is a "split", in the language of homology the birth of a new class.

The truth of this dataset is not an observation but a construction: the event list was written by the scheduler before any computation, and the Betti curve was computed by an independent reference implementation from the snapshots written to disk. A Task 5 test compares the two sources.

The index convention, without which everything below shifts by one: the record "snapshot $k$" means that $G_k$ already contains the change and $G_{k-1}$ does not yet. The jump of the curve falls on the transition $k-1 \to k$.

The second dataset, geometric_loop, is built in a fundamentally different way: each frame holds distances between 24 points on a circle, and the graph is built by a Rips complex. The radius of the circle breathes, and the arc opens and closes according to a schedule.

In [4]:
def loop_points(snapshot, n=24):
    """The points of a frame are recovered from the distance matrix only for the picture."""
    d = LOOP.snapshots[snapshot]
    # multidimensional scaling into two dimensions: the classical Torgerson formula
    sq = d ** 2
    j = np.eye(n) - np.ones((n, n)) / n
    b = -0.5 * j @ sq @ j
    values, vectors = np.linalg.eigh(b)
    order = np.argsort(values)[::-1][:2]
    return vectors[:, order] * np.sqrt(np.maximum(values[order], 0))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(13.5, 3.2))
for ax, (snap, title) in zip(axes, [(0, "0: arc closed\n$\\beta_1 = 1$"),
                                    (20, "20: gap opened\ndeath of $H_1$"),
                                    (43, "43: radius breathes\nNO event"),
                                    (45, "45: gap closed\nbirth of $H_1$")]):
    pts, adj = loop_points(snap), graph_at(LOOP, snap)
    for i, j2 in zip(*np.triu_indices(24, 1)):
        if adj[i, j2]:
            ax.plot(*pts[[i, j2]].T, color="tab:blue", lw=0.7, zorder=2)
    ax.scatter(*pts.T, s=14, color="0.25", zorder=3)
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=8.5); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("geometric_loop: a metric dataset, a Rips complex on every frame",
             y=1.06, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The third panel is the main negative control of the metric dataset. At snapshot 43 the graph changes substantially (45 edges against 66), but $\beta$ does not, and there is no event. A detector that fires on any change of the complex is caught exactly here. There are three such snapshots — 4, 43 and 56 — and they are checked by name.

2. Why ordinary persistence is not enough here¶

In the Task 5 report the filtration always grew: the scale $\varepsilon$ increased, simplices were only added, and the inclusion $K_{\varepsilon} \subseteq K_{\varepsilon'}$ went one way. All of ordinary persistence rests on this.

A dynamic graph does not behave like that. Between neighbouring snapshots edges both appear and disappear, so neither $G_i \subseteq G_{i+1}$ nor the reverse inclusion holds in general.

In [5]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 2.9), sharey=False)
for ax, (ds, name) in zip(axes, [(LIFECYCLE, "cycle_lifecycle"), (LOOP, "geometric_loop")]):
    counts = [int(graph_at(ds, t).sum() // 2) for t in range(len(ds.snapshots))]
    ax.step(range(len(counts)), counts, where="post", color=PALETTE(3), lw=1.6)
    for t in range(1, len(counts)):
        if counts[t] != counts[t - 1]:
            ax.annotate("", xy=(t, counts[t]), xytext=(t, counts[t - 1]),
                        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color="0.4", lw=0.8))
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: number of edges per snapshot", fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel("snapshot"); ax.set_ylabel("edges")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("The number of edges both grows and falls. An ordinary filtration needs monotonicity;")
print("there is none here, so a different construction is needed.")

The number of edges both grows and falls. An ordinary filtration needs monotonicity;
there is none here, so a different construction is needed.

The way out is zigzag persistence: a sequence whose arrows alternate direction. Between neighbouring snapshots their union is placed, and both snapshots include into it:

$$K_0 \hookrightarrow K_0 \cup K_1 \hookleftarrow K_1 \hookrightarrow K_1 \cup K_2 \hookleftarrow \cdots \hookleftarrow K_{T-1}$$

Now every arrow is an honest inclusion, and the algebra works: such a diagram is a representation of a quiver of type $A_N$, and by Gabriel's theorem its indecomposable summands are exactly the interval modules. So the barcode is uniquely defined and does not depend on the algorithm used to compute it.

In [6]:
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 2.4))

kinds = ["snapshot", "union", "snapshot", "union", "snapshot", ""]
for k, (text, kind) in enumerate(zip(labels, kinds)):
    colour = PALETTE(0) if kind == "snapshot" else (PALETTE(1) if kind else "white")
    ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((k * 2 - 0.55, -0.32), 1.1, 0.64, facecolor=colour,
                               alpha=0.22, edgecolor=colour if kind else "white", lw=1.4))

    if kind:
        ax.text(k * 2, -0.55, kind, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5, color="0.4")

            fontsize=8, color="0.35")
for k in range(5):
    forward = k % 2 == 0
    x0, x1 = (k * 2 + 0.6, k * 2 + 1.4) if forward else (k * 2 + 1.4, k * 2 + 0.6)
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, 0), xytext=(x0, 0),
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color="0.35", lw=1.3))
ax.text(5, 0.85, "indices $I$: integers are snapshots, half-integers are unions",
        ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color="0.3")
ax.set_xlim(-1.2, 11.2); ax.set_ylim(-0.9, 1.1); ax.axis("off")
ax.set_title("The zigzag construction: arrows alternate direction", fontsize=9.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

2.1. The union of complexes, not the flag complex of the union of graphs¶

A fork that looks like a detail of notation and is not one. It is always true that $\mathrm{Fl}(G_i) \cup \mathrm{Fl}(G_j) \subseteq \mathrm{Fl}(G_i \cup G_j)$, and in general strictly: three edges of a triangle lying in different snapshots give a triangle on the right and not on the left.

The simplexwise union is adopted, and not for convenience: an intermediate object must not contain a simplex that exists in no snapshot. Otherwise such a triangle kills a cycle at an intermediate index, and the barcode acquires a "birth–death" pair that corresponds to no state of the data — while the barcode remains self-consistent, and no test will dispute it.

The difference was measured and turned out to be zero on all 59 transitions of both datasets. This is recorded as a measurement, not as the ground for the choice: the rule rests on the principle and will survive the first dataset with different geometry.

3. Indices: why bar ends can be half-integer¶

The least obvious place of the construction, and the one where the specification was wrong.

Closing the path at snapshot 12 is an addition of an edge. So $K_{11} \subseteq K_{12}$, and the union $K_{11\frac12} = K_{11} \cup K_{12}$ coincides with $K_{12}$. The cycle already exists there, i.e. the class is born at index $11\frac12$, not 12.

In [7]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(11, 3.2))
draw_graph(axes[0], graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 11), "$K_{11}$: a path\n$\\beta_1 = 0$")
union = np.maximum(graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 11), graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 12))
draw_graph(axes[1], union, "$K_{11½} = K_{11}\\cup K_{12}$\n$\\beta_1 = 1$  ← the class is already here",
           highlight=((0, 23),))
draw_graph(axes[2], graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 12), "$K_{12}$: a cycle\n$\\beta_1 = 1$")
fig.suptitle("Adding an edge: the union coincides with the NEXT snapshot",
             y=1.04, fontsize=9.5)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

before = int(graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 11).sum() // 2)
after = int(graph_at(LIFECYCLE, 12).sum() // 2)
print(f"edges in K_11: {before};  in the union K_11½: {int(union.sum() // 2)};  in K_12: {after}")
print("the union coincides with the next snapshot, so the class already lives at 11½")

edges in K_11: 23;  in the union K_11½: 24;  in K_12: 24
the union coincides with the next snapshot, so the class already lives at 11½

For a death the sign is the opposite. Removing the edge $(6,7)$ at snapshot 41 means $K_{41} \subseteq K_{40}$, so the union $K_{40\frac12}$ coincides with the previous snapshot, and the dying class survives until $40\frac12$.

For $H_0$ everything is reversed: the birth comes from removing an edge (a component detaches at 48), the death from adding one (the edge is restored at 55), and in both cases the union coincides with the previous snapshot. Hence the integer ends.

That is, a half-integer end is neither an error nor a choice but a consequence of the direction in which the transition is monotone. An earlier edition of the specification wrote these bars in snapshot indices and was wrong by half a step; corrected by measurement.

4. The answer is computed twice, by different methods¶

The inviolable point of the whole task: the oracle is built before the backend. If a zigzag persistence library came first, it would become its own reference, and the first index-translation error would be fixed as truth.

So an independent oracle was written first. It does not implement a zigzag algorithm at all; it computes the barcode from the definition of the invariant: for each interval $[b,d]$ it takes the rank of the canonical map from the limit to the colimit,

$$r(b,d) = \operatorname{rank}\bigl(\varprojlim V|_{[b,d]} \to \varinjlim V|_{[b,d]}\bigr),$$

and the multiplicities of the bars are recovered by Möbius inversion. Over $\mathbb{Z}/2$ both constructions are ranks of Boolean matrices, and there is no persistence library here.

Only after that did Dionysus 2 appear. A second backend is not a check: it repeats the same class of algorithm and cannot say which one is right when they disagree. The oracle is the check.

Blue — the two clean datasets, grey — the sixteen noisy ones. Checking agreement only where the barcode has four bars would be the weakest possible version of the claim: an adapter error — the order of operations, the presence intervals of a simplex, the translation of a half-open end — is more likely to show up where a dataset gives nine hundred bars. This is most of the cost of make results, and the part worth paying for.

Before the datasets, the adapter was validated on toys whose barcode is written out by hand. One of them, T3, is a miniature of the fork of section 6: two layouts with identical coverings, and Dionysus picks the right one.

5. The barcode¶

Each bar is an interval on the index set $I$: the class was born at the left end and survived to the right one. The report prints indices the way the documents write them: 12 for a snapshot, 11½ for the union between 11 and 12.

cycle_lifecycle:

The four bars of cycle_lifecycle and its five events match like this: three births (12, 27, 48) are visible; the birth of the infinite $H_0$ bar is left-censored — the class already existed when observation began; the deaths of the bars $[26½, 59]$ and $[0,59]$ are right-censored — the window ended first.

In geometric_loop the second $H_1$ bar cannot be a continuation of the first: there is no class at all between snapshots 20 and 44, and intervals are connected. This is the substantive difference between "the loop came back" in the language of graphs and two different classes in the language of homology.

6. Pairing: why the death at 41 belongs to the birth at 12¶

The subtlest claim of the whole task, and the one where intuition fails.

After the chord is added there are two classes in $H_1$, and at snapshot 41 one of them dies. Which one? The tempting answer: "the chord created a second cycle, we break an edge of one of them — the younger dies". This is wrong. The class that dies is the one born when the path closed, i.e. the pair 12↔41.

And this is not a convention that can be assigned: the decomposition of a zigzag module into intervals is unique (Gabriel, Krull–Schmidt), and the answer depends on which edge exactly is removed — i.e. it is determined by geometry. It is checked by computation: at the vertex, the class brought in from the left and the class surviving to the right span different lines of a two-dimensional space, so the space splits into a direct sum, and the bar on the left does not go past the vertex.

In [10]:
cl = CLEAN["cycle_lifecycle"]
bars = cl["barcode"]["1"]
births = sorted(b for b, _ in bars); deaths = sorted(d for _, d in bars)
correct = [(births[0], deaths[0]), (births[1], deaths[1])]
crossed = [(births[0], deaths[1]), (births[1], deaths[0])]

def betti_from(pairing, n=119):
    return [sum(1 for b, d in pairing if b <= p <= d) for p in range(n)]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 4.0), sharex=True,
                         gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1, 1]})
for col, (pairing, title, ok) in enumerate(
        [(correct, "the right layout (the one the algorithm gives)", True),
         (crossed, "the crossed layout", False)]):
    ax = axes[0, col]
    for k, (b, d) in enumerate(pairing):
        ax.plot([b / 2, d / 2], [-k, -k], lw=7, solid_capstyle="butt",
                color=PALETTE(2) if ok else PALETTE(3))
        ax.annotate(f"[{label(b)}, {label(d)}]", (d / 2 + 0.6, -k), va="center", fontsize=7.5)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.7, 0.7); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9, color="0.15" if ok else "0.45")
    axes[1, col].step(range(119), [v / 1 for v in betti_from(pairing)], where="post",
                      color="0.3", lw=1.5)
    axes[1, col].set_ylim(-0.2, 2.4); axes[1, col].set_xlabel("position on $I$")
    axes[1, col].set_title("Betti curve of $H_1$", fontsize=8.5)
fig.suptitle("Two layouts, ONE Betti curve: L1 is blind to pairing", y=1.02, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Betti curves coincide:", betti_from(correct) == betti_from(crossed))
print("barcodes differ      :", sorted(correct) != sorted(crossed))
print()
print("The algorithm chose:", ", ".join(f"[{label(b)}, {label(d)}]" for b, d in sorted(bars)))

Betti curves coincide: True
barcodes differ      : True

The algorithm chose: [11½, 40½], [26½, 59]

Both layouts give the same Betti curve and the same arrow ranks. Only the full invariant tells them apart — the generalised rank with Möbius inversion from section 4.

This is the third occurrence of one and the same blindness in the project. In Task 5 the Betti curve did not distinguish pairing; here the vertex and arrow coverings do not; and section 8 will show that the event log does not either.

7. From the barcode to the event log¶

A bar lives on $I$, while the truth log speaks about snapshots. The translation is two asymmetric rules:

  • a birth goes to the first snapshot index not earlier than the birth of the bar;
  • a death goes to the first snapshot index strictly later than its death.

The familiar shift $d \mapsto d+1$ is the second half of the rule at an integer end, not a separate rule. It is introduced in exactly one place in the code and has its own test: an off-by-one here looks in the report like a systematic localisation error of the algorithm and is indistinguishable from one.

An earlier edition of the specification sent half-integer ends to a special category "event in transition". A measurement showed that the log is not recovered this way: in cycle_lifecycle both $H_1$ bars have half-integer ends, and the rule would give "in transition" where the truth records an ordinary birth at 12 and death at 41.

In [11]:

8. Result 2: the metrics — and what they do not check¶

Matching happens only within a (type, dimension) pair, with a tolerance $\tau$ in snapshot index. The default is $\tau = 0$: only an exact coincidence can match.

In [12]:
print(f"{'dataset':<18}{'recall':<9}{'precision':<12}{'|dt| max':<10}{'by dimension'}")
for name, e in CLEAN.items():
    m = e["metrics"]
    per = "  ".join(f"H_{d}: {v['n_matched']}/{v['n_truth']}"
                    for d, v in sorted(m["by_dimension"].items()) if v["n_truth"])
    print(f"{name:<18}{m['recall']:<9.3f}{m['precision']:<12.3f}"
          f"{m['max_localisation_error']:<10}{per}")

dataset           recall   precision   |dt| max  by dimension
cycle_lifecycle   1.000    1.000       0         H_0: 2/2  H_1: 3/3
geometric_loop    1.000    1.000       0         H_1: 2/2

The ones here are an expected outcome, not an achievement. The datasets are built so that the answer is known in advance, and the algorithm is exact; it would be strange to get anything else. The value of the metric lies in the fact that under noise it stops being one (section 11), and the report, not the reader, must say so.

The metrics are computed separately by dimension, and this is not a formality: the five events of cycle_lifecycle split into three in $H_1$ and two in $H_0$, and a pooled recall would hide an algorithm flawless in one dimension and blind in the other.

The localisation error at $\tau = 0$ is identically zero — only an exact hit can match. It is published because the specification requires it, but it is not an informative quantity. Measured: on eight noisy datasets raising the tolerance to one recovers one event in one of them, i.e. under noise the failure is omission and a flood of false events, not displacement.

Censored events are marked and do not enter the metrics. A censored birth does not claim that a class was born; it says the class already existed when the window opened. Counting it as a false positive would penalise the algorithm for the finiteness of observation.

8.1. The boundary of Result 2¶

An event does not remember which bar it was derived from. So the right $H_1$ layout and the crossed one from section 6 give bitwise the same event log, and recall and precision do not check the 12↔41 pair. The barcode comparison of section 4 checks it.

In [13]:
def events_of(pairing, n=119):
    out = []
    for b, d in pairing:
        if b > 0:
            out.append((next(p for p in range(b, n) if p % 2 == 0) // 2, "birth"))
        if d < n - 1:
            out.append((next(p for p in range(d + 1, n) if p % 2 == 0) // 2, "death"))
    return sorted(out)

print("right layout     ->", events_of(correct))
print("crossed layout   ->", events_of(crossed))
print()
print("logs coincide:", events_of(correct) == events_of(crossed))
print()
print("So recall and precision do NOT confirm the 12<->41 pair.")
print("The barcode comparison confirms it: 3192 bars, 0 discrepancies (section 4).")

right layout     -> [(12, 'birth'), (27, 'birth'), (41, 'death')]
crossed layout   -> [(12, 'birth'), (27, 'birth'), (41, 'death')]

logs coincide: True

So recall and precision do NOT confirm the 12<->41 pair.
The barcode comparison confirms it: 3192 bars, 0 discrepancies (section 4).

This is the same blindness as the Betti curve's in Task 5 and the coverings' in section 6, one level further: curve → coverings → event log. Each next level of reporting loses pairing anew, and the report has to say so rather than imply it.

9. Four quantities that are counted and recorded¶

None of them is silently discarded, because each one characterises the construction, not implementation noise.

In [14]:
print(f"{'dataset':<18}{'invisible':<11}{'censored':<10}{'from half-int':<15}"
      f"{'ephemeral (prologue + outside)'}")
for name, e in CLEAN.items():
    k = e["counters"]
    print(f"{name:<18}{k['invisible_bars']:<11}{k['censored_ends']:<10}"
          f"{k['events_from_half_integer_ends']:<15}"
          f"{k['ephemeral_bars']} = {k['ephemeral_in_prologue']} + "
          f"{k['ephemeral_outside_prologue']}")

dataset           invisible  censored  from half-int  ephemeral (prologue + outside)
cycle_lifecycle   0          3         3              23 = 23 + 0
geometric_loop    0          4         2              165 = 71 + 94

An invisible bar contains no snapshot index in its support: the class exists in no state of the data, it lives only on a union. Such a bar is a false positive by construction. On the clean datasets there are none, and that is a measurement, not a default.

A censored end touches the boundary of the sequence: the class already existed when observation began, or still existed when it ended.

An event from a half-integer end is a diagnostic of the union construction. In cycle_lifecycle three events of five are derived from a half-integer end, in geometric_loop both.

An ephemeral bar is born and dies within one transition. The coarse path and the oracle cannot see them by construction: no index of the diagram catches them. They are visible only on the fine path, where the backend is given one time per operation rather than per index.

And here a caveat matters. The number is published decomposed into the prologue and the rest, because the prologue part measures not the data but the assembly order of the first complex: building a 24-cycle from the empty complex gives birth to 24 components and kills 23 of them. This order is fixed lexicographically and is arbitrary in substance.

10. The null model: a measurement, not a check for zero¶

The null model has no schedule and an empty event log, so any event is a false positive. The right answer is not "zero false positives" but a rate with the number of trials and a confidence interval.

This is a lesson from Task 5, and it took a separate analysis there: three seeds that gave zero misses bound the true rate by 63 percent, not by zero. A zero without a denominator is not a result.

ER at the density of cycle_lifecycle, 3 seeds x 20 realisations
  per snapshot     0.9833  (3540/3600, 95% Wilson [0.9786, 0.9870])
  per realisation  1.0000  (60/60, 95% Wilson [0.9398, 1.0000])
  events: 46323 (H_0: 25710, H_1: 20613)
  per snapshot: 12.9

Every snapshot of the null model is a topological event. This is not a defect of the algorithm: a random graph at this density honestly has $\beta_0 = 4\ldots5$ and $\beta_1 = 2\ldots5$ on every snapshot, and the edges are redrawn independently, so classes are born and die continuously.

Both denominators are published, because neither on its own is honest. Per snapshot is what the specification requires, but the trials there are not independent: neighbouring complexes share edges, and the interval is narrower than the true one. Per realisation the trials are independent, but there are sixty of them, and the interval is wide. The number of events per snapshot goes as a third row, because the rate of 0.98 is saturated and says nothing about scale.

The threshold null_models.max_false_positive_rate does not apply here, although it has exactly that name. It was calibrated for the significance criterion on the Task 5 clouds — the fraction of realisations in which the criterion invented a feature, 1.5% with a bound of 4.3%. The zigzag measures the fraction of snapshots that fire. Comparing them would declare failure while measuring different quantities.

plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Three observations, each visible in the figure.

Recall falls slowly, precision collapses. For cycle_lifecycle the precision reaches 0.17%: the algorithm loses events less than it floods the log with false ones. The failure under noise is not a shift in time but a deluge.

geometric_loop keeps recall at one at every level. Both of its events are always found; only the precision deteriorates. This is a property of the datasets, not measurement noise, and a summary over sixteen rows would hide it.

spurious_edges is an order of magnitude more harmful than missing_edges. An added edge creates cycles; a removed one most often merely breaks an existing one.

Level 0.0 reproduces the clean dataset exactly — a free check that catches at once a wrongly connected base, a shift of the random stream between levels and an unconditional clip.

The prologue part drifts by units (23 → 28 and 71 → 87), while the part outside it grows by orders of magnitude (0 → 857 and 94 → 1567). At zero noise the sum consists entirely of the prologue, so without the decomposition the zero reference point would be false, and "the growth of the number of ephemeral bars under noise" would be measured from the wrong starting point.

12. Limits of applicability¶

They have to be named, because each is a place where a number from this report stops meaning anything.

The barcode depends on the union convention. Barcodes obtained under different conventions are not comparable. So the convention lies in the artefact itself, next to the bars, rather than being inferred from the commit in which the file appeared.

In [19]:
c = ART["convention"]
print(f"union rule          : {c['union_rule']}")
print(f"coefficient field   : Z/{c['coeff_field']}")
print(f"dimension           : up to H_{c['max_homology_dim']}")
print(f"backend             : {c['backend']}")
print(f"matching tolerance  : tau = {c['event_matching']['tolerance']}")
print()
print(c["index_convention"])

union rule          : complex_union
coefficient field   : Z/2
dimension           : up to H_1
backend             : dionysus
matching tolerance  : tau = 0

barcodes live on I = {0, 1/2, 1, ..., T-1}: integer positions are snapshots, half-integer ones the unions between them. An event is placed on the first snapshot index at or after a birth and strictly after a death (docs/zigzag.md 4.2).

Truncation of the complex. Complexes are built up to dimension $k_{\max}+1$, and bars of dimension $k_{\max}$ are reliable. Higher dimensions are not computed, and their absence from the output is not a claim of their absence in the data.

The backend does return such bars — on the metric dataset there are 69 of them in $H_2$ — and the adapter cuts them off. That these are artefacts and not a finding is not known by default: the generator built its complexes one dimension higher, with the necessary boundary operator, and recorded $\beta_2 = 0$ on every snapshot. The 69 bars contradict a number that was computed correctly.

Bar significance in the zigzag is not defined. The criterion parameters from Task 5 are not inherited here: they were calibrated on point clouds, and, moreover, the criterion is not invariant under reparametrisation of the filtration. No replacement is introduced in this branch — and section 10 shows that the question is not academic: without a criterion the precision on noise falls to 0.17%, and on the null model 98% of snapshots fire.

The localisation error at $\tau = 0$ carries no information (section 8).

Briefly, by layer — so that the reader can see where to look in the code.

layer       what it does                                  how it is checked
core        contracts, config, reading datasets           the edge rule has one implementation
reference   homology over Z/2, zigzag oracle              toys with the answer written by hand
zigzag      complexes, operation stream, backend, events  stream replay, agreement with the oracle

artefact: 18 datasets, 3192 bars compared, 0 discrepancies
content hash: 6be89481b849170e5db7e22ea0d17e9a2143f7c8950cf27cde006a6c1a25d145

Dependencies between layers go one way: the layer that produces the truth does not know about the layer that consumes it. zigzag does not import the generators — it reads datasets through core; reference imports neither. The single exception is named and checked by a test: tdadyn.results is the composition root, which needs both layers and therefore stands above them rather than inside one.

Three test targets: make fast (without zigzag backends, 16 s), make slow (Task 5 topology, about ten minutes), make zigzag (oracle and backend, 5:43 — of which 4:46 is the single rebuild of the artefact in the hash reproducibility test).

14. What next¶
Vineyards track the movement of diagram points under a continuous change of the filtration: points crawl, cross and swap. The zigzag here is discrete by construction — nothing happens between an integer and a half-integer index that could be tracked continuously. This is a different object, not postponed work, and it is needed where the filtration is continuous: Task 3 and the bifiltration of Result 3
Bar significance is posed anew and is not solved by tuning a threshold to precision
Connectomes the numbers of invisible and ephemeral bars from section 9 are what must be known before transferring: both are false positives by construction of the union
Open item the slow run grew during Task 2 from 10:10 to 10:48 against a guideline of 15 minutes; four minutes of headroom are left, and the cure will be to split targets, not to weaken the checks
